body:
Why observations are arranged in tables and graphs

Measurements often become easier to compare when organised into a table or graph. A table gives exact recorded values. A graph makes changes, relative sizes and patterns visible. Neither can compensate for incorrectly measured or misleading data.

Before interpreting a graph, identify its title, the quantities shown, the horizontal axis (x-axis), the vertical axis (y-axis), the units and the scale. A scale tells how much change in the actual quantity each marked interval represents.

Reading a distance–time graph

Consider this illustrative journey. A vehicle's cumulative distance travelled is represented by straight segments between the following recorded points:

Elapsed time (min)Total distance travelled (km)
00
102
204
304
408

Time is on the x-axis and cumulative distance on the y-axis. Between 0 and 20 minutes, the plotted distance rises by 2 km in every 10-minute interval. On the straight portions representing those intervals, the vehicle moves at a uniform speed of 12 km/h. Between 20 and 30 minutes the horizontal segment means no further distance is covered, so the vehicle is stationary during that plotted interval. Between 30 and 40 minutes the line rises more steeply: 4 km in 10 minutes, representing 24 km/h.

The steepness or slope of a distance–time line expresses how quickly distance changes with time. A steeper upward straight line indicates greater speed. A straight rising line indicates uniform speed over that segment; a horizontal line indicates no increase in distance. If only the 5 table readings were known, the vehicle could have varied its speed between readings. The straight segments are therefore an additional assumption of this illustrative graph, not a fact established by the table alone.

Read the exact quantity on the y-axis. Cumulative distance travelled cannot decrease. Distance from a fixed starting point, however, can decrease if someone returns towards that point. These are not the same graph.

Bar charts compare categories

A bar chart is useful for comparing separate places or categories, while a line graph is especially useful for showing change across ordered times. Suppose the recorded rainfall on the same day at 3 imaginary weather stations in Gujarat is: Station A, 10 mm; Station B, 25 mm; and Station C, 15 mm. A bar chart shows that Station B received the most, and B received 15 mm more than A. These figures are invented learning data, not reported observations.

For a bar chart, a scale beginning at zero usually helps readers compare amounts fairly; a truncated vertical scale can exaggerate differences. The axis units also matter: 25 mm of rainfall is not the same quantity as 25 °C of temperature.

What a graph cannot establish

A graph can display a measured relationship, but it does not automatically establish why that relationship occurs. A rising line does not alone prove a causal mechanism. Apparent patterns should be interpreted using the source of the measurements, their time period, the units and possible alternative explanations.

Prelims focus

  • Read graph axes, units, intervals and scale before comparing values.
  • A table presents recorded values; a graph makes trends and comparisons easier to see.
  • In a cumulative distance–time graph, a horizontal segment means zero distance added in that interval.
  • A steeper upward straight segment means greater uniform speed over that segment.
  • Bar charts compare categories; line graphs commonly show change with time.
  • Trap: A trend shown on a graph does not by itself prove a cause.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', printed pp. 151–155, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', Section 8.4, 'Graphical Representation of Motion', printed pp. 104–106, 2018–19 printing. All rainfall and journey values on this page are illustrative, not observed data.]

body:
Move from a statement to a justified conclusion

Scientific reasoning connects a claim to observations that can actually test it. The main questions are whether the claim is specific, whether appropriate evidence has been obtained, whether measurements are comparable and whether the conclusion stays within what the evidence shows. Careful wording is essential: a result may support a claim under particular conditions without establishing that it always holds.

A worked example: comparing the growth of seedlings

Suppose 2 groups of similar seedlings are grown for 7 days. Group A receives 2 hours of sunlight each day, while Group B receives 6 hours. Both groups receive 100 mL of water daily and have similar initial size, soil and containers. The following are invented measurements for explanation, not the results of a real experiment.

GroupLight per dayHeight gained in 7 days
A2 h2 cm
B6 h4 cm

Here, the observation is that Group B gained 4 cm while Group A gained 2 cm. The proposed explanation is that increased sunlight contributed to greater height gain. The comparison is consistent with that explanation, but one small comparison does not justify the claim that every plant always grows twice as fast with more sunlight. Other relevant conditions, including temperature, may differ. Repeated comparisons would make the conclusion more dependable.

A stronger conclusion is: 'Under the stated conditions, the group receiving 6 hours of sunlight per day gained 2 cm more height over 7 days than the group receiving 2 hours.' It reports what was observed without claiming more than the evidence shows.

Check the claim against the type of evidence

  • One unusual event: A single day's high temperature does not establish a long-term climate trend; the claim concerns a much longer period than the observation.
  • Wrong comparison: Values measured in cm and m must be converted to the same unit before their sizes are compared.
  • Misleading display: A dramatic-looking bar chart may exaggerate a small numerical change if its scale is cut short.
  • Unwarranted cause: Two events occurring together do not, without further support, establish that one caused the other.
  • Incomplete evidence: A photograph showing clear-looking water does not establish that it is safe to drink; appearance alone cannot rule out invisible contaminants.

These distinctions work together. A clear hypothesis guides observation; standard units make results comparable; a well-labelled table or graph reveals the recorded pattern; and a careful conclusion distinguishes what the evidence establishes from what remains uncertain.

Prelims focus

  • A testable claim is stronger than an uncheckable assertion because its prediction can be examined.
  • A fair comparison limits other changing factors; repeated results can improve confidence.
  • Always compare measurements using compatible units and stated time periods.
  • A graph summarises observations but cannot by itself establish causation.
  • Trap: 'Supported in this comparison' does not mean 'proven true for every case'.

[Sources: NCERT, Curiosity, Class 6, Chapter 1, printed pp. 5–7 (chapter transcription consulted on NCERT Solutions website, 2 November 2026); NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', printed pp. 151–155, 2018–19 printing; Smithsonian Learning Lab, Next Generation Science Standards, 'Planning and Carrying Out Investigations', grades 3–5 guidance (consulted 2 November 2026). Worked seedling values are illustrative.]
